newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan decries China's U.N. moves in Latin America.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan decries China's U.N. moves in Latin America.

text.p: Taiwan on Thursday slammed rival China for using its U.N. Security Council seat to squeeze Latin American states that recognise Taipei as worries mounted over secretive Chinese-Guatemalan talks in New York.

"We should altogether condemn communist China's acts of using its influence in the U.N. Security Council to interfere in the internal affairs of Central and South American countries," said Foreign Ministry deputy spokesman Chen Yung-tso.

Chen said he knew little about a closed-door meeting at U.N. headquarters on Wednesday between diplomats from Beijing and Guatemala, which recognises Taipei's exiled Republic of China rather than the communist People's Republic on the mainland.
"We need further checks," Chen said without elaborating.

U.N. diplomats said China had requested the meeting in a bid to repair the effects of its controversial veto that barred U.N. observers from monitoring a Guatemalan peace pact. The meeting was likely to continue on Thursday, diplomats said.

The fact that China and Guatemala were talking despite a lack of diplomatic ties fuelled worries on Taiwan that Beijing might succeed in tempting Guatemala to follow South Africa's recent example and sever ties with Taipei in favour of Beijing.
"We are facing tremendous pressure on the diplomatic front," a senior government analyst said in a telephone interview on condition his name not be used.

"Communist China can use its power at the Security Council to force Guatemala to make certain concessions," he said. "It will depend on how badly Guatemala wants the U.N. peacekeepers. The Security Council seat is a very powerful weapon."
Guatemalan diplomats in Taipei declined to take calls.
Fourteen of 15 council members on Friday voted in support of sending 155 military observers to Guatemala to monitor U.N.-brokered peace pacts that ended a three-decade civil war.

China, using its council veto for the first time in its 25 years as a member, blocked the mission because of Guatemala's ties to Taiwan, its support of Taipei's drive for U.N. membership and its invitation to Taiwan's foreign minister to attend a December 29 peace accord signing.
China's U.N. ambassador, Qin Huasun, said last week Beijing might reconsider if Guatemala "moves to remove the obstacles" -- a clear appeal for it to drop recognition of Taipei.

Beijing, which has regarded Taiwan as a renegade province since a civil war split them in 1949, has tightened a diplomatic embargo around the island by stepping up pressure on Taiwan's handful of diplomatic partners to switch allegiance.
South Africa -- which like Guatemala is among just 30 states that recognise Taipei, not Beijing -- shocked Taiwan in November by pledging to switch to Beijing this year. No date has been set.
Wealthy but diplomatically isolated Taiwan gives considerable economic aid to its remaining allies, mostly poor states in Africa and Latin America, to ensure their allegiance.
President Lee Teng-hui and other Taiwan leaders have voiced confidence in ties with Guatemala and said the island would do "whatever it can" to help its Central American ally.
The rival Chinas' foreign ministers have been touring Africa this week in separate drives to win support and undermine each other's influence on the continent.
Taiwan lost the sole U.N. China seat to Beijing in 1971.
